source.title: Controlling Refusal Behavior of LLMs via Stiefel-Constrained Rotation Steering
source.authors: Kirill Bunin; Dmitry Bylinkin; Vladimir Aletov; D. Medyakov; V. Solodkin; A. Beznosikov

page_placements.theme: Directions and maps other than DIM also control refusal; DIM is not the unique or optimal handle

record.tranche_reason: The study uses refusal-direction and steering work as motivation, then develops and evaluates its own learned-rotation attack and defense. It does not remove or add the difference-in-means direction, or test whether that direction mediates refusal.
record.gate_note: The paper compares learned rotation steering with other methods and measures unsafe-response rates and capability metrics. Those outcomes concern the paper's own rotation intervention, not the claim's difference-in-means direction. Figure 4 compares learned activation trajectories with an estimated refusal direction, but the authors explicitly say this does not establish that a single direction is insufficient. Values used to choose configurations and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper builds and evaluates its own learned Stiefel-subspace rotation (StiefelSteer). The difference-in-means refusal direction never enters the operator; it is used only for layer-selection scoring and for one figure comparison. No row ablates or adds that direction, and none tests whether it mediates refusal. Table 1 includes Angular Steering, a refusal-direction-plane rotation, and RDO, but only as baselines for the authors' method. Figure 4 compares learned trajectories with the DIM direction, and the authors say this does not show a single direction is insufficient.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that StiefelSteer controls refusal in both directions, with near-unmodified capability in nearly all cells, and that estimating the refusal direction is not necessary. They stop short of calling a single direction insufficient, because unrelated directions are near-orthogonal in d=3584; settling this would need a constrained-rotation control. Note that the introduction overstates this, saying the structure 'extends well beyond the refusal direction'.
record.recipe_differences: The original uses a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and tests projection/steering of that direction. This paper learns Stiefel-subspace rotations with a behavioral loss and uses an inverse rotation for defense; the refusal direction is not part of the transformation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rotation effect varies with model, attack versus defense regime, judge, variant, and number of intervened layers. On DeepSeek-R1-7B, the layer sweep reports one layer as insufficient and two layers as sufficient for the reported effect; the paper also sweeps rotation-subspace dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: A learned rotation in a ~35-dim subspace across 2 layers drives unsafe rates to 0.86–0.99 (attack) and 0.00–0.01 (defence) on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, with ARC and perplexity near baseline. On Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE it elicits 0.78–0.97 unsafe.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal can be controlled by a learned low-dimensional rotation without estimating the refusal direction, with small capability cost.

fits_no_version.finding: On a base model with no safety tuning, the inverse rotation reduces unsafe rates from 0.73 to 0.20–0.29 (Llama-Guard) and from 0.70 to 0.29–0.36 (Qwen3Guard).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned rotations can induce refusal in base models lacking safety training.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned rotation trajectories end far from the DIM refusal direction. The authors call this evidence of sufficiency, not of necessity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective refusal control need not follow the DIM direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Unmodified-model keyword refusal counts, including 12/50 refusals on harmless prompts for Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE.

record.code_released: Code is included with the submission; no URL stated.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported Table 1 values. The defensive intervention is trained and evaluated on the same harmful-prompt distribution; the authors say they do not test adaptive attacks or measure over-refusal after defense. Only three checkpoints between 1.5B and 7B are tested. The paper notes that high unsafe scores can reflect degenerate text for a comparator method; it reports capability metrics to address this concern for its own methods.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 reports additional benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Easy, GSM8K) for the Table 1 configurations; those capability outcomes are not extracted here because the 60-row budget was reserved for the main safety and capability results plus the directly reported refusal counts. Figure 2 and Figure 3 sweeps are also omitted: the paper describes those as parameter-selection/sensitivity experiments, and their detailed curves are not needed to record the main outcomes. Cited findings from other work are excluded.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the DIM direction; no capability check of direction ablation.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No controlled test of affine, cone, or multi-direction structure. The authors explicitly decline to infer it from Figure 4.
Keyword refusal and judge-labelled harmfulness are reported separately, but harm and refusal representations are not tested.
No cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test.
Models differ in alignment stage, but the paper does not test whether training determines a removable direction.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill is a reasoning model, but the DIM-direction intervention is not tested on it.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 baselines are not extracted, correctly, since they compare the authors' method with others. Angular Steering and RDO elicit 0.00 unsafe on Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE under attack, and Angular Steering rotates within a refusal-direction plane. That failure of direction-based steering on a hardened model might interest V3/V7 readers, but it is a best-configuration baseline, not a DIM ablation test. Falcon3-7B-Base's 0.73 baseline unsafe rate is partly degenerate text, not compliance (Appendix B.1/B.6).

versions.untested_parts: No ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction; the rotation results do not test whether it mediates refusal or whether ablating it preserves capabilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No jailbreak suppression of the direction or training against its ablation.
The trajectory comparison is not a controlled test of whether refusal is affine, a cone, or multiple directions; the authors say it does not establish that a single direction is insufficient.
The paper reports separate unsafe and keyword-refusal measurements, but does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal decision.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct direction-transfer test.
Models with different alignment stages are included, but the study does not test how refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
A reasoning-distilled model is included, but the study does not test the single-direction intervention in reasoning models.

relation.reason: The difference-in-means direction is used as a tool (layer selection, Figure 4 comparison), and the DIM-based Angular Steering appears only as a baseline. No result tests whether that direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: The paper reports its own learned-rotation method against baselines. The DIM direction enters only as a layer-selection score and as the reference in Figure 4. No DIM ablation or addition is run, and the authors explicitly decline to read their results as evidence on a single direction.

source_check.notes: The intro (lines 64-65) claims steered activations are 'nearly orthogonal' and that safety structure 'extends well beyond the refusal direction', with no number. Sec 5.5 and the conclusion retract this, so use the caveated reading. Single-direction and DIM-based baselines (RDO, Angular Steering) elicit 0.00 unsafe on Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE. That is not a DIM ablation, so it tests no version. States on the version-none rows follow the record's method-effect convention. Sec 4.2 (defence retrained with refusal targets) and Sec 5.2 (defence = M^T) disagree about how defence works.

statements.correction: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, L=2, n=35. Attack unsafe rate 0.86-0.90 (Llama-Guard, from 0.52) and 0.98-0.99 (Qwen3Guard, from 0.71). Defence 0.00-0.01 on both judges. ARC-Challenge 0.39-0.42 vs 0.40 baseline. Perplexity 24.5-26.8 vs 26.4, except 29.2 for the Cayley attack. Figure 4 (figure only, 3-PC projection): trajectories end far from the DIM direction, but the authors say near-orthogonality is the default at d=3584, so this does not show that one direction is insufficient.
statements.problem: The numbers are right: n=35, L=2, attack 0.86-0.99, defence 0.00-0.01. But perplexity is not near baseline in every cell: it rose 26.4->29.2 under the Cayley attack, the exception the authors themselves flag. The trajectory sentence also leaves out the authors' caveat that this separation is expected by default and is not evidence against a single direction.
